characterList.description: A young, white, Australian drummer with short brown hair and a light beard. He wears a green shirt over a white T-shirt, jeans, red sneakers, and a gray flat cap. Later in the video, he takes off the shirt and is wearing a sleeveless white shirt.
characterList.name: Ben Walsh

content_metadata.description: The video covers Ben Walsh's presentation at TEDx Sydney, where he shares his journey as an innovative drummer using a custom-built drum set.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: All right, welcome back to the space. Welcome to the people in the foyer as well. There's
a whole another festival going out there and they've got a bar. And I'd like to firstly
apologize to all the scientists. No, I haven't discovered a time portal. I'm going to let
you down straight away. My name is Ben Walsh, I'm a drummer and this little drum contraption
I'm about to play for you. You could try to look this up online and you wouldn't find
any explanation at all. So I decided I'd like to just talk to you for a second about how
I got to this point of time. Basically about 35 years ago I was born in a little town in
the central coast of New South Wales called Gospherd. It's very synonymous with drumming
at all. And before I could talk I had the urge to drum to hit things. My parents heard
a huge crash in the kitchen one day and they came down. Oh no, what's happened? There
was with pots and pans banging them together. Stole a couple of cake tins, took them upstairs,
wouldn't give them back. Primary school show and tell was a drum kit. High school was
all the bands touring around in illegal bars with pub bands like no worries and things
like this. High school, same university. Now I'm a drummer. And that's what I've always
been. I can never think of a day where I have an accept of the fact that I'm an artist,
a musician. Just recently I was in Womad which is a fantastic festival and I was on stage
with some phenomenal musicians and drummers from all over the world. And I was confronted
by one of them. He took me aside and he said, what are you doing here? And I said, what
do you mean? He said, well, you're a young white Australian drummer. What do you have culturally
to bring to the table? What can you offer? It kind of shocked me. I was a bit hurt but
I'm really glad it happened because it culminated in me kind of searching, being an artist
in Australia at this time is quite difficult, especially in musician. When we think about
what can we really add to the why of wanting to be an artist is there but the how? What
can we truly add? What can we do in this day and age that hasn't been done? How can we
communicate? And so I started to slowly evolve this kind of concepts. One of the things
I do. And I've always built things out of junk and you can see this is not a traditional
thing I'm about to do here by any sense of the word. These drums are made of rubbish but
I'm giving them another fantastic purpose right about now. And taking the waist and taking
a whole bunch of techniques and in that void, I guess cultural void, they were I existed.
I discovered some fantastic techniques and through my I am a sponge for music. I love
any type of big drum, little drum, whatever instrument. I love it and don't get me wrong,
I'm not against tradition by any means. But I discovered some interesting techniques,
this multi-directional drum form that I've now taken from the humble streets of Newtown
and Macville from the reverse garbage where I bought these barrels all the way to Broadway,
all over the world. I've been touring this for five years people and I'm so excited
to play it for you today. And thank you. And hey, I'm not, this is not a big self-inflated
moment. No, I'd like to dedicate this right about now to all the people with a small idea
in a big city that seems too difficult or a big idea in a small country town that you
think, what am I thinking about? Just go for it. Dive into the deep end people, into that
creative pool, explore the void, enjoy the void. And like I said, I'm not against tradition,
so I'd like to leave a little speech and play this for you now, but I'd like to leave
with this all tradition is sacred and totally deserves our respect. But how can a tradition
form? How can it be passed on without the spirit of invention and exploration? Thank you.

youtube_description:
Ben Walsh's diverse percussion and drumming skills have made him a fixture at festivals around the world. Here, he tells us a little of his story and proceeds to demonstrate his art on a 'wheel of drums' he created.
http://tedxsydney.com/site/newSpeakers.cfm#BenWalsh
-------------------

TEDxSydney 2011 took place on Saturday 28 May 2011 at CarriageWorks. Tens of thousands of people enjoyed the day: 800 in the theatre, over 1,000 via big screen simulcast in The Forum, up to 48,000 online via YouTube ... and up to 80,000 tuning in to ABC Radio National. It was a grand day.

About TEDx, x = independently organised event

In the spirit of ideas worth spreading, TEDx is a program of local, self-organised events that bring people together to share a TED-like experience. At a TEDx event, TEDTalks video and live speakers combine to spark deep discussion and connection in a small group. These local, self-organised events are branded TEDx, where x = independently organised TED event. The TED Conference provides general guidance for the TEDx program, but individual TEDx events are self-organised.* (*Subject to certain rules and regulations)
